title: Year three close: the story and the circle
hook: a long line from Jericho to Lagos, and a year that keeps turning

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Andrew, who found his brother and brought him. Your line was we have found him. Who did you invite to something good? Day one thousand sixty-one.

Twelve stones, piled up near Jericho. Each was carried up out of a river on a man's shoulder, from the dry riverbed where the priests stood, one man for each tribe. Joshua tells them the stones are for the children. That was near the start of this year: Israel crossing the Jordan. From there the story ran a long line, through judges and kings, exile and return, apostles and martyrs, monks and reformers, all the way to churches in Lagos. Then the line bent into a circle, and walked the church's year of feasts, from Advent candles to a king crowned with thorns. Today, both close. Today's word: Year three close.

This year had two shapes. The first was a line. Israel's story from Joshua to the return from exile. The early church, its martyrs and its creeds. The middle centuries, east and west: cathedrals and crusades, mystics and plague. The reformations, Protestant and Catholic, with saints and failures on both sides. Then the church spreading across the world, to Lagos and far beyond. A line has a direction. It says: this happened, then this, and it matters what came first. The second shape was a circle. For these last weeks we walked the church year: Advent and Christmas, Lent and Easter, Pentecost, saints' days, All Souls, Christ the King. A circle doesn't go anywhere. It comes round again. In Western churches, the first Advent candle will soon be lit again. Ecclesiastes knew both shapes: "One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever." The generations are the line. The earth, and its seasons, are the circle. Go back to those stones by the Jordan. Joshua says they are a sign, so that "when your children ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean ye by these stones?" someone will tell them the story. That's how the line keeps going: a child asks, and someone answers. And that's why the circle matters: every year the feasts come round, the questions get asked again, and the story gets told again. The psalm puts it in one breath: "One generation shall praise thy works to another." Neither shape is finished. The line hasn't ended. The circle keeps turning. And somewhere on both of them, there's a spot marked today.

Here's the practice: write your place in the story. Settle, and breathe. Let the year pass by: the river and the stones, the prophets, the apostles, the monks, the reformers, the churches in Lagos, the candles and feasts. Then ask where you are in it today. Inside it, beside it, at the door, still deciding. All of those are places. Find one honest sentence that says where you stand. When the bell ends, write it down. If you pray, you can offer that sentence to God. If you don't, just keep it. The bell holds the time.
Year three close. The end of the long story: a line from Jericho to Lagos, and a circle of feasts that keeps turning.

Your line: the circle turns. Put your sentence somewhere you'll find it next year, like a stone by the river. Tomorrow, year four begins: many rooms, and how people talk about God. Day one thousand sixty-one.

howItsDone: Western churches that follow the church year mark its turning at Advent (the Orthodox year begins on 1 September), and some end the old year with Christ the King and begin the new one with the first Advent candle, telling the same story again.

notes: Editor pass: the hook no longer has a man 'wade' into the river (Joshua 3:17 and 4:3 say the riverbed was dry, where the priests' feet stood); it now opens on the stones themselves, to vary from three scene openings in a row; 'crowded' cut from the Lagos churches. 'Twelve' and 'one man for each tribe' follow Joshua 4:2–5.
Year close: summarizes the year's blocks (A–F of y3.md) and points to year four, 'many rooms', starting with day 1062 'Talking about God'.
'Eleven others do the same' follows Joshua 4:2–5 (twelve men, one from each tribe); the stones are set up at Gilgal near Jericho (Joshua 4:19–20). 'Near Jericho' is a simplification; confirm.
'Near the start of this year' refers to day 699 (Twelve stones), not day 697. Confirm wording.
Ecclesiastes 1:4 is read here as 'line and circle'; interpretive, offered as a picture. Confirm.
Avoided Hebrews 12:1 (cloud of witnesses), already used for the day 1001 block close.
'Soon the first Advent candle will be lit again' assumes the listener follows the church calendar; the app's calendar may not align. Consider softening.

Audit pass (serious): the myth item and howItsDone said the church year starts again at Advent without qualification; on this broad path that is Western only (the Orthodox church year begins 1 September, the Indiction). Now says 'in Western churches' and names the Orthodox start. Confirm. The older note about 'Eleven others do the same' refers to wording no longer in the hook.
